# Apple Human Interface Guidelines

Use the relevant Apple guidance to make concrete design decisions. This package
contains a router, 13 family routes, 158 operational topic skills, and supporting
article-level references. It is
independent of Apple. The sources are a dated English HIG snapshot; check the
official source when a task depends on a newer release or a disputed detail.

## Route the task

1. Identify the target platform, device context, and user task from the request or
   project. Ask for the platform only when it materially affects the answer and
   cannot be inferred. Preserve the user's framework and product requirements.
2. Select the relevant family below and read that family's `SKILL.md`. Follow its
   link to the exact topic procedure under `.topics/` and read that `SKILL.md`.
   Apply its decision procedure, then consult its supporting article for facts
   and platform qualifications. Topic skills are explicitly read by installed
   file path; automatic nested discovery is not required.
   For platform support, product feasibility, or platform adaptation, first read each relevant
   platform's Getting started procedure, then the specific component or technology
   procedure. Check both the platform model and the surface's support limits.
3. Before finalizing the route, search the [complete topic index](references/topic-index.md)
   for the task's concepts as well as component or framework names. Its trigger
   descriptions connect everyday product requests to Apple's topic names; users
   need not name an Apple framework. Read the owning family and matching topic
   procedure before its supporting reference. Search relevant rows instead of
   loading the full corpus for a narrow question.
   For a screenshot-specific or animated example, also consult its
   [original visual explanation](references/media/index.md) when available.
4. Apply shared guidance and the target platform's documented differences. A
   missing platform subsection means no additional rule is stated; it does not
   prove support, nonapplicability, or identical behavior across platforms.
5. Compose families when the task crosses them: a component can also require
   accessibility, typography, localization, input, or system-experience guidance.
   Map the brief's material decisions to their owning topics. Read the owning
   procedure for each explicit concern, such as privacy or accessibility, as well
   as the affected components; a neighboring procedure's reminder is insufficient.
   Use [platform and task routes](references/platforms-and-tasks.md) when useful.
   In a review, map each supplied control to its candidate component procedure
   even when markup or behavior is missing. Use it to frame inspection questions;
   missing evidence neither proves a defect nor removes that control from scope.

All paths are relative to **this installed package**, not the shell's current
directory. No Python, network, sibling skill installation, or authoring cache is
required to read the guidance.

| Task | Read this topic skill |

| Platform conventions, design principles, games, device adaptation | [Getting started](subskills/apple-hig-getting-started/SKILL.md) |
| Accessibility, typography, color, materials, layout, localization, privacy | [Foundations](subskills/apple-hig-foundations/SKILL.md) |

| Alerts, sheets, popovers, panels, scrolling and windows | [Presentation](subskills/apple-hig-presentation/SKILL.md) |
| Text fields, pickers, sliders, toggles, selection controls | [Selection and input](subskills/apple-hig-selection-and-input/SKILL.md) |
| Progress, activity, gauges and ratings | [Status](subskills/apple-hig-status/SKILL.md) |
| Widgets, Live Activities, notifications, Siri snippets and system surfaces | [System experiences](subskills/apple-hig-system-experiences/SKILL.md) |

| Apple Pay, purchases, Siri, VoiceOver, AI, CarPlay and integrations | [Technologies](subskills/apple-hig-technologies/SKILL.md) |

## Perform the requested work

Inspect the supplied brief, flow, code, specification or image before deciding
what is wrong or choosing a framework. Use the user's requested mode:

- **Design:** produce an implementable specification or interaction/state model
  from the topic's decision procedure, with concrete transitions and acceptance
  checks. Connect choices to the user's task and target platform.
- **Implement:** prefer the project's native system components when they supply
  the needed behavior. HIG explains experience requirements; verify API names,
  availability, and code against the appropriate SDK documentation. Make the
  authorized changes in the existing stack; a prose explanation alone does not
  complete an implementation request.
- **Review:** describe the observed problem, its effect, the relevant HIG rule,
  and a concrete correction. Separate source-backed findings from your own
  suggested improvements. Do not invent violations without inspecting evidence.
- **Adapt:** preserve the product task, data and useful state while applying the
  destination platform's interaction model. Patch the supplied artifact or give
  an explicit before/after contract when a design specification is requested.

Topic procedures are framework agnostic. Their worked examples and pseudocode
teach decisions, not a requirement to replace the project's technology. Load
related procedures only for a decision that actually depends on them.

Complete the topic's observable checks and report passed, failed and not executed
separately. Reading a file, citing Apple, or proposing a test does not establish
runtime behavior. Static code or screenshots cannot prove assistive-technology
order, native rendering, physical comfort, haptics, or SDK compilation.

Include official article/section links for material recommendations. Preserve
qualifications such as “consider,” “prefer,” and “avoid”; do not turn design
advice into invented universal requirements. Retain units and platform scope for
numerical specifications. If source passages conflict, describe the conflict
and the conservative application rather than silently changing the source.

## Source boundaries

This is comprehensive local guidance, not a verbatim Apple manual or an SDK API
reference. Original media explanations are supplementary to article references;
the source page remains useful for visual demonstrations. Source snapshots and
review status live in the repository's coverage report, outside ordinary skill
loading. Do not infer that a source has been independently reviewed just because
its local file exists.

Historical `navigation-bars` links now resolve to current Toolbars guidance;
`in-app-purchase` resolves to Apple In-App Purchase. The old Touch Bar and Messages
for Business HIG pages were unavailable at this snapshot. Do not fabricate their
current rules. Translations, archived pages, and complete linked SDK/WWDC libraries
are outside the source boundary.

name: apple-hig-designing-for-watchos
description: Use when creating, reviewing, or adapting an Apple Watch experience for brief glances, focused actions, complications, wrist-down states, and independence from iPhone.
---

# Fit the task to a wrist glance

Read [Designing for watchOS](../../references/designing-for-watchos.md). Inspect the proposed Watch task, frequency, urgency, companion-phone dependency, and supplied screens. Identify the information needed at wrist raise and the action worth performing there. Choose design, review, or adaptation mode; produce the requested revised artifact rather than transplanting the whole phone app.

Separate a glance from deeper interaction. Put the useful value and next action on one screen when possible, keeping navigation shallow and gestures few. Use the Digital Crown for vertical movement rather than requiring repeated precise swipes. If a task needs prolonged text entry or broad comparisons, simplify its Watch responsibility and provide a coherent continuation elsewhere without making the entire Watch app merely a remote notice.

Choose entrypoints by purpose: a complication supplies recurring glance value and opens the corresponding context; a timely notification should let people act without launching; an Action button suits an essential action useful without looking. Do not require sensor access just because the device provides sensors. Personalize only with an explained task benefit and appropriate permission.

Design wrist-up and Always On information together, including what remains useful and what should become less prominent. Provide independently useful app detail beyond the complication or notification. Preserve progress when the wrist lowers or an interruption occurs.

**Worked transformation:** Before, a tea timer copies a phone recipe browser and requires four screens before starting. Decision: the wrist task is checking and controlling the current steep. After, the first screen shows remaining time and a large Pause/Resume action; Crown navigation reaches saved presets, and a complication opens the running timer directly. The phone retains detailed recipe editing.

Deliver a glance/action flow, entrypoint destinations, and wrist-state behavior or implementation. Fail if a complication opens unrelated content, a routine action requires deep navigation, or lowering the wrist loses the timer. State whether actual Watch readability, Crown response, notification handling, and sensor access were tested; static evidence cannot prove them.

Continue with [Digital Crown](../../../apple-hig-inputs/.topics/apple-hig-digital-crown/SKILL.md), [Always On](../../../apple-hig-technologies/.topics/apple-hig-always-on/SKILL.md), or [Action button](../../../apple-hig-inputs/.topics/apple-hig-action-button/SKILL.md) only for the selected interaction.

# Designing for watchOS Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/designing-for-watchos) · Retrieved 2026-10-25. This is original application guidance based on the source text. Independent media review is recorded separately in the coverage report. Apple Watch serves brief glances and focused actions while people are still or moving. The small, dense display is typically within about a foot when the wrist is raised. Always On also communicates when the wrist is lowered; many interactions last less than a minute. ## Best practices - Give the most useful information and action on a single glanceable screen, ideally requiring only one or two gestures. - Keep navigation shallow. Use the Digital Crown for vertical scrolling or moving among screens; support familiar taps, swipes, and drags. - Provide relevant actions through complications, notifications, Siri, and Shortcuts, which people may use more often than the app itself. - Use the Action button for a suitable essential action that can be performed without looking. - With appropriate access, personalize timely content using GPS, heart and blood-oxygen sensors, altitude, acceleration, and rotation data. - Make complications useful on every wrist raise and let a tap enter the right app context. Keep notifications timely, valuable, and actionable without requiring an app launch. - Use backgrounds and color to communicate supporting context and materials to clarify hierarchy and place. - Build an independently useful watch app that provides the extra detail and functionality beyond its notifications and complications. Integrate Always On and watch-face expectations. ## Resources Consult the [official article](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/designing-for-watchos) for linked Apple design assets and implementation resources. #### Related The official article links the adjacent HIG topics relevant to this guidance. #### Developer documentation Use the framework references linked by Apple for current API availability and implementation details. #### Videos Apple’s linked design sessions provide demonstrations and additional implementation context; no video review is implied here. ## Change log Source revision dates: June 5, 2023.

name: apple-hig-pickers
description: Use when creating, reviewing, or adapting ordered value choices, date or time entry, and multipart picker behavior.
---

# Match the choice structure to its scale

Read [the picker guide](../../references/pickers.md). This workflow is application advice; consult the source for supported date styles/modes rather than assuming every combination works.

Inspect the option count/order, value constraints, locale/calendar/time zone needs, platform/input, and create/review/adapt mode. Establish whether the task is selecting an instant, date, duration, or ordinary option. Record stored semantics separately from displayed formatting.

Use a picker for medium/long ordered lists, simpler controls for short sets, and searchable/indexed layouts for very large datasets. Put it near the edited value and arrange hidden choices predictably. For minute intervals choose a divisor of 60. On iOS/iPadOS select a supported date style/mode combination: countdown cannot use inline/compact and has a bounded duration. Let locale determine order instead of hardcoding month/day assumptions. On Mac choose textual precision versus graphical calendar browsing. On watch choose Crown-friendly wheels or navigation-link lists. Do not invent unsupported API behavior in the user's stack.

Implement the value/display/commit behavior, supply a concrete choice/date specification, or review exact constraint and locale failures. Define invalid/out-of-range incoming values without silently changing the person's meaning.

**Worked transformation:** Before: a scheduling form hardcodes month/day/year, uses 7-minute wheel steps, and offers a compact countdown. Decision: order must localize, minute steps must divide 60, and the chosen mode/style is unsupported. After: use locale ordering, a suitable interval such as 5 minutes, and an allowed duration presentation.

Deliver the artifact, ordered choices, stored semantics, bounds, and commit policy. Verify locale/calendar changes, boundary values, keyboard entry where supported, and edits/cancellation. Fail for a wrong date meaning, unreachable valid option, unsupported mode/style, or silent constraint violation. Separate logic checks from native calendar/Crown/keyboard execution.

Use [pop-up-buttons](../../../apple-hig-menus-and-actions/.topics/apple-hig-pop-up-buttons/SKILL.md) for compact single choice or [lists-and-tables](../../../apple-hig-layout-and-organization/.topics/apple-hig-lists-and-tables/SKILL.md) for very large sets.

# Pickers Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/pickers) Snapshot: 2026-10-25. Original implementation guidance derived from the source. Pickers offer scrollable, ordered choices for single or multipart values. Language and locale affect displayed values and order. Date pickers can also use calendars and numeric entry. ## Best practices Use a picker for a medium or longer list. A short list may work better in a pull-down; a very large dataset may need a resizable list or indexed table. Arrange values logically so hidden choices are predictable, for example alphabetically. Present the picker near the edited field, commonly at the bottom of the window or in a popover, instead of forcing a separate navigation step. Minute wheels default to 0–59. A coarser interval is allowed if it divides 60 evenly; 15-minute steps produce 0, 15, 30, and 45. ## Platform considerations visionOS has no additional rules in this source. ### iOS, iPadOS Date entry supports touch, hardware keyboards, and pointers. Choose among these styles: | Style | Presentation | | --- | --- | | Compact | Current value in an accent-colored button; activation opens a modal calendar/time editor | | Inline | Calendar for dates and dates with time; a time-only button reveals wheels | | Wheels | Scrolling value wheels with built-in or hardware keyboard entry | | Automatic | The system chooses for the platform and mode | Modes are date (month/day/year), time (hour/minute and optional AM/PM), date with time, and countdown (hours/minutes, maximum 23 hours 59 minutes). Countdown is unavailable with inline and compact styles. The exact ordering follows device location. Compact is useful for tight space and permits multiple date/time edits before tapping outside to confirm. ### macOS A textual picker saves space and supports precise entry. A graphical picker suits calendar browsing, date-range selection, or a clock-face presentation. ### tvOS SwiftUI Picker provides picker support. ### watchOS The Digital Crown enables precise movement through choices. Wheel styles support ordinary values and dates/times; configure outlines, captions, and scroll indicators as needed. For longer lists, a navigation-link picker displays a button that opens the list, and also allows crown scrubbing without opening it. ## Resources Official implementation links and revision metadata follow. #### Related [Pull-down buttons](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/pull-down-buttons) [Lists and tables](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/lists-and-tables) #### Developer documentation — SwiftUI — UIKit — UIKit — AppKit ## Change log Revision dates recorded by Apple: June 5, 2023.

name: apple-hig-digital-crown
description: Use when designing or reviewing Watch Crown navigation or adjustment, touch equivalents, detents, or the system-owned Vision Pro Crown behavior.
---

# Assign Crown rotation without conflicting with navigation

Read [Digital Crown](../../references/digital-crown.md). Identify Watch versus Vision Pro, the current scroll/navigation context, any adjustable value, and requested design/review/adaptation. Preserve the stack and inspect actual state transitions rather than assuming every hardware rotation can become an app command.

On Vision Pro, retain the system's volume, immersion, recentering, accessibility, and Home behavior; do not map these controls to arbitrary application actions. On Watch, reserve Crown presses for the system. Since watchOS 10, rotation is the main navigation mechanism, so use it for adjustment only where it is not already needed to navigate.

Define which visible content responds and how touch performs an equivalent operation. Keep the response visibly connected to rotation. Tune change rate to speed while retaining precise selection; a fast turn may cover a range quickly, but a slow turn must settle on a value. Choose appropriate default haptic detents, avoiding conflicting taps/animation. For variable-height rows, consistent linear detents can be more predictable than treating every row as equal physical distance.

**Worked transformation:** Before, a Watch altitude history simultaneously scrolls the page and changes a selected day on Crown rotation, with no touch alternative. Decision: the same rotation cannot ambiguously navigate and adjust. After, the main page uses rotation for scrolling; entering an explicit day-inspection view adjusts the highlighted day with visible values and an equivalent touch selector, then returns to the prior scroll position.

Deliver a context-to-rotation mapping, response/rate rules, touch equivalent, and corrected artifact. # Digital Crown Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/digital-crown) · Retrieved 2026-10-25. This is original application guidance based on the source text. Independent media review is recorded separately in the coverage report. The Digital Crown provides system interaction on Vision Pro and Watch, and app interaction on Watch. ## Apple Vision Pro The system uses the Crown for volume, immersion amount in portals/Environments/Full Space, recentering, Accessibility settings, and exiting to Home View. Do not assume these are arbitrary app inputs. ## Apple Watch Since watchOS 10, Crown rotation is the main navigation mechanism: Smart Stack on the face, vertical app browsing on Home, vertical paginated tabs, lists, and variable-height pages in apps. Provide equivalent touch navigation. Use rotation for data inspection or control adjustment where it is not needed for navigation. Crown presses are reserved by the system. Always show a corresponding visual response. Match the rate of UI change to rotation speed while preserving precise selection. Use default haptic detents where they fit; disable them if animation and taps conflict. Tables can use row-based or linear detents; varying row heights can favor consistent linear feedback. ## Platform considerations The source marks it unsupported on iOS, iPadOS, macOS, and tvOS. ## Resources Consult the [official article](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/digital-crown) for linked Apple design assets and implementation resources. #### Related The official article links the adjacent HIG topics relevant to this guidance. #### Developer documentation Use the framework references linked by Apple for current API availability and implementation details. ## Change log Source revision dates: December 5, 2023, June 21, 2023, June 5, 2023.

# Apple HIG: Commands, roles and discoverable surfaces

Use this family to select and compose topic procedures. Infer the platform and
requested work from the supplied project; preserve its framework and constraints.

## Work through the decision

1. Inventory each command’s outcome, scope, availability and reversibility. Distinguish immediate commands from persistent selection before entering Buttons, Toggles, or the appropriate menu procedure.
2. Choose a discoverable primary surface plus contextual shortcuts. On Mac, consider the menu bar’s command catalog and keyboard access even when a toolbar or context menu also exposes the action.
3. Use consequence and current task to decide role/default, confirmation and recovery. Consult Alerts and Undo and redo when that decision depends on destructive behavior; preserve documented exceptions.
4. Deliver an action contract naming labels, roles, surfaces, shortcuts, availability and relevant pending/resolved behavior. Verify the action and its recovery rather than color alone.

# Operate on buttons

Read [the buttons guide](../../references/buttons.md) before making HIG claims. This procedure is application advice for turning that guide into an artifact; platform facts and dimensions come from the guide. Preserve the user's framework and authorized scope.

## Establish the action contract

Inspect the supplied screen, code, prototype, or brief. Identify the target platform, input methods, surrounding task, and requested mode: create, review, or adapt. For each consequential button, record its visible label or symbol, activation outcome, affected object, reversibility, current role/default status, and actual hit region if available. A screenshot can establish visible styling; it cannot establish hit geometry, keyboard behavior, or accessible names. Mark those as unknown and inspect implementation when available.

Classify the action before styling it. An immediate command fits a button. A persistent on/off setting may need a toggle; choosing one of several persistent options may need a segmented control or picker; a menu-opening control needs the corresponding menu button behavior. Retain a button when its action is to open that choice, but distinguish opening from committing a choice.

## Make and apply the consequential choices

1. Write an outcome-specific short verb phrase, or use a familiar symbol whose meaning survives its context. Give an icon-only control an accessible name that states the action. Do not assume a tooltip replaces the name. On Mac, an ellipsis indicates that another window, view, or app requires further input; add it based on the continuation, not merely because an operation takes time.
2. Assign semantic roles from consequences. Prefer one or two prominent likely actions per view and use style rather than unequal sizes to rank related choices. A primary/default action should normally be the likely nondestructive choice. If destruction is involved, consult the alerts topic before deciding confirmation and Return behavior: the guide explicitly allows a deliberate-destruction alert exception, so “destructive can never be default” is not a universal rule. Cancel abandons the current task; it is not a generic label for completing it.
3. Choose the system control/style when available, retaining its states and accessibility behavior. For a custom control, specify perceivable press feedback and preserve meaningful focus, enabled/disabled, and selected states as applicable. State the reason for a disabled action when the surrounding context does not explain it. This is application advice, not a new Apple requirement to add all states to every button.
4. Check visual and selectable geometry separately. Apply the guide's target and separation rules for the actual platform; a small glyph or small visual style does not establish a small hit region. On visionOS, retain a discernible shape/fill, use standard audible/state feedback, and inspect center spacing and hover overlap. Do not propose unsupported custom hover effects or haptics there. On watchOS, choose inline versus toolbar placement deliberately; preserve common heights for peer controls and use short labels for side-by-side actions. On Mac, distinguish view-body square/image/help buttons from toolbar items; apply the help-button placement/count rules only when designing Help.
5. Only when the command has delayed completion, define the initiating, waiting, and resolved behavior. On iOS/iPadOS, use the activating button's activity indication as described in the guide, preserving context and replacing its image when appropriate. Specify how duplicate activation is handled and what success or failure means in the product; do not promise network completion from a press animation.

Perform the authorized work: implement the controls in the supplied project for a build request; produce an annotated control specification for a design request; or report evidence-backed defects and exact corrections for a review. For adaptation, map each affected control to its destination platform rather than copying appearance alone.

## Deliver and verify

Return the changed artifact or a compact button contract containing label/name, outcome, role/default, style/placement, target region, and relevant state behavior. In review mode attach findings to identifiable controls and separate observed defects from checks requiring execution.

Verify that activation reaches the named outcome; cancellation leaves the intended prior state; keyboard/default activation cannot commit an unintended outcome; focus and accessible names identify the action; and enlarged labels do not clip or overlap adjacent targets. Measure hit regions from layout/runtime data when available. Fail the design if a destructive consequence is mislabeled, peer targets overlap, an icon has no discoverable name, or custom press feedback is absent. State separately which checks were inspected in source, exercised, or remain Apple-device checks; Linux inspection does not prove gaze, VoiceOver, haptics, or native rendering.

## Worked transformation

**Before:** A Mac photo organizer has equally prominent `Go`, `Remove`, and `Close` buttons. `Go` opens export settings; `Remove` deletes a selection with undo; `Close` finishes editing metadata.

**Decision:** The labels hide three different contracts. Export requires further input; routine reversible removal does not by itself justify a confirmation alert; finishing edits should name completion. The export task, rather than removal, is the likely action on this screen.

**After:** Specify `Export…` as the prominent action opening export settings, `Remove Photos` as a lower-emphasis command with a visible Undo path, and `Done` for finishing metadata edits. Inspect actual save semantics before changing `Close` to `Done`. Verify the Return mapping, undo restoration, and that each accessible name matches the resulting action. These product choices are an example application, not facts about the unseen implementation.

## Conditional handoffs

Load alerts for consequential confirmation/default decisions; toggles or segmented-controls for persistent selection; pop-up-buttons or pull-down-buttons for menu-opening behavior; toolbars when placement belongs to window chrome; and accessibility when naming, focus, contrast, or target access needs deeper work. Keep this button contract as the input to the next topic.

# Buttons Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/buttons) Snapshot: 2026-10-25. Original implementation guidance derived from the source. ## Contents - [Best practices](#Best-practices) - [Style](#Style) - [Content](#Content) - [Role](#Role) - [Platform considerations](#Platform-considerations) A button performs an immediate action. Its visual style, visible symbol/text, and semantic role work together to explain what activation does. ## Best practices Allow enough surrounding space for clear separation and easy selection. General hit regions should be at least 44×44 pt; visionOS targets need 60×60 pt. Custom buttons always need press feedback. ## Style Prefer system styles for built-in states, accessibility, and appearance adaptation. Use one or two prominent buttons per view for likely actions. Distinguish a preferred option through style rather than making related buttons different sizes. Keep label colors distinct from colorful content; the default monochrome often works best over rich backgrounds. ## Content Use a familiar symbol for a familiar action; use a short title-case verb phrase when words are clearer. Mac and visionOS can provide brief hover tooltips; text-labeled buttons usually explain themselves. ## Role Normal has no special meaning; primary is the expected/default action; Cancel abandons the current action; destructive signals data loss. Roles affect rendering, such as accent fill for primary and red for destructive. Primary can respond to Return and close a temporary view. Generally assign primary only to a nondestructive likely action. Application advice: consult the alert-specific deliberate-destruction exception before prescribing confirmation behavior. ## Platform considerations No additional tvOS rules are specified. ### iOS, iPadOS For delayed completion, show an activity indicator within the activating button, optionally changing its label to the current operation. The indicator replaces any button image while preserving context for the wait. ### macOS #### Push buttons The standard push button can show text, imagery, or both and can serve as default. Use flexible height for tall icons or multiple text lines, otherwise retain standard sizing. Append an ellipsis when the button opens another window/view/app for further input. Consider spring loading through a dragged selection plus force-click on Magic Trackpad, preserving the drag afterward. #### Square buttons These small glyph-only controls affect a nearby view, for example adding/removing table rows. They can act as push, toggle, or pop-up controls. Use them in the body rather than the frame, toolbar, or status bar. Prefer system symbols and omit introductory labels when proximity explains the function. #### Help buttons Use the familiar system question-mark control, at most one per window, opening context-specific help when possible and top-level help otherwise. In a dialog with dismissal controls, place it in the opposite lower corner, aligned vertically with those controls. Without dismissal controls, or in settings, use either lower corner. Keep it in the view body and omit explanatory introductory text. #### Image buttons Image buttons can act as push, toggle, or pop-up controls inside a view. Toolbar imagery instead belongs to a toolbar item. Allow about 10 pixels between image and clickable button edges and generally omit a visible system border. Put any needed label beneath the image. ### visionOS Buttons normally have a visible background and audible feedback. Circle suits glyph-only content, rounded rectangle or capsule suits text, and capsule suits text plus glyph. Standard states supply feedback; custom hover effects are not supported. A look-triggered tooltip can explain a glyph. | Shape | Supported visual sizes | | --- | --- | | Circle | Mini 28 pt; small 32 pt; regular 44 pt; large 52 pt; extra large 64 pt | | Text capsule | Small 32 pt; regular 44 pt; large 52 pt | | Text-and-icon capsule | Regular 44 pt; large 52 pt | | Rounded rectangle | Small 32 pt; regular 44 pt; large 52 pt | Visual size does not remove the 60-pt targeting requirement. Use a discernible shape/fill except inside a larger clearly bounded toolbar, menu, alert, or ornament. On window glass, thin material suits the button; floating in space, use glass. Reserve white fill with black content for the system's toggled state. Prefer round/capsule forms for steady gaze, and a capsule for a standalone button. Keep centers at least 60 pt apart; add 4 pt padding around buttons 60 pt or larger to prevent hover overlap. Avoid rows/stacks of mini/small buttons. Prefer rounded rectangles for vertical text stacks and capsules for horizontal rows. Standard sounds matter because visionOS provides no haptics. ### watchOS Inline buttons are capsules with a contrasting material. Put corner actions in a toolbar so the system relocates title/time and gives controls Liquid Glass. Full-width buttons suit primary actions. Side-by-side buttons should share height and use short labels or glyphs; vertical one- and two-line buttons should also maintain common heights. Toolbar actions can navigate related areas or operate on current content. ## Resources Official implementation links and revision metadata follow. #### Related [Pop-up buttons](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/pop-up-buttons) [Pull-down buttons](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/pull-down-buttons) [Toggles](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/toggles) [Segmented controls](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/segmented-controls) [Location button](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/privacy#Location-button) #### Developer documentation — SwiftUI — UIKit — AppKit ## Change log Revision dates recorded by Apple: December 16, 2025, June 9, 2025, February 2, 2024, December 5, 2023, June 21, 2023, June 5, 2023.

item.text: The brief needs a time of day and repeat schedule, so I won’t add a calendar date field. I’ll replace the 1,440-item picker with labeled hour and minute wheels, make “Every day” explicit, and specify how edits survive Crown turns and interruptions.

# Watch medication reminder — revised specification

Platform: watchOS. Task: edit one medication reminder's time of day and a small named repeat schedule. No framework is specified. This is a control and state contract, not SDK code.

## Summary and editing flow

The reminder editor shows the medication name, "'`Time` with a localized time value, and `Repeat` with the selected schedule name. Each labeled row opens its editor in one tap. Keep navigation one level deep. Use system watchOS controls; allow vertical scrolling when content does not fit.

The product needs a recurring time, not a calendar date or duration. Do not add a date/calendar picker. A start date or one-off reminder would require a separate product requirement.

## Time control

Replace the 1,440 unlabeled minute options with a watchOS wheel-style time editor. Provide clearly captioned Hour and Minute components and an AM/PM component when the locale uses a 12-hour clock. Show the complete localized time above the wheels. Use locale conventions for component order and displayed digits.

- Preserve all 1,440 daily minute values: minutes 00–59 in one-minute steps; hours 00–23 for 24-hour display or 1–12 plus AM/PM for 12-hour display. One minute divides 60 and preserves existing precision.
- Store hour 0–23 and minute 0–59 separately from localized labels. This is a recurring local wall-clock time, not an absolute timestamp or a countdown.
- Tapping a component makes it the sole active wheel, indicated by the system selection outline. Crown rotation adjusts only that component; it never resets the draft, changes Repeat, or scrolls the enclosing page at the same time. Touch dragging provides equivalent wheel selection.
- Retain system wheel behavior and default haptic feedback where appropriate. Slow Crown movement must permit selecting each minute; faster movement may traverse values more quickly. Do not repurpose Crown presses.
- Component boundaries wrap within the selected component without carrying to another: minute 59 → 00 leaves hour and AM/PM unchanged. Display the resulting complete time immediately.

## Repeat control

Use a labeled system single-selection picker presented as a short navigation-link list, with the current value visible in the summary. Choices appear in this fixed order:

| Stored identifier | Visible label | Eligible local days |
| --- | --- | --- |
| daily | Every day | Monday–Sunday |
| weekdays | Weekdays | Monday–Friday |
| weekends | Weekends | Saturday–Sunday |

These three presets are a concrete product assumption for this revision, not an Apple requirement or a clinical recommendation. Localize names and include the day range beneath Weekdays and Weekends so regional interpretations are explicit. Every option has visible text; no blank row, placeholder, or implicit “Every day.” Show the selected option with the system selection indicator. Selecting an option updates the draft and returns to the summary. Back without selecting preserves the prior draft.

The short named list avoids a numeric frequency wheel and permits direct touch selection. In the summary, Crown rotation scrolls only; merely focusing Repeat must not scrub its value. Within the opened list, rotation navigates choices; selection requires activation. If the chosen native navigation-link picker scrubs the bound value from its closed row, isolate it in the explicit Repeat editor so it cannot change the summary inadvertently.

## State, defaults, and committing

- On edit, initialize the draft once from the saved hour, minute, and repeat identifier. Crown events mutate that draft rather than reconstructing it. Reopening either subeditor starts at its current draft value.
- For a new reminder, propose the current local time rounded down to the minute and Every day; display both for review. This is a proposed reminder configuration, not dosage advice.
- Time editor `Done` accepts its local changes into the reminder draft; `Cancel` or Back restores the time at entry. These actions are system text buttons. Repeat selection changes only the draft.
- The summary has a full-width primary `Save` button and a secondary `Cancel` button, vertically arranged with consistent peer heights and separated targets. Use standard watchOS inline button styles. Save commits the complete draft; Cancel discards it. No wheel movement schedules a reminder.
- Save returns to reminder detail only after persistence succeeds. On failure, retain the draft, explain that saving failed, and offer Save again. Prevent duplicate saves while one is pending. Cancel never changes the saved reminder.
- Retain draft values, active component, and navigation position across wrist lowering and interruptions. Returning must not silently save, reset, or replace user input with a default.
- Accept only integer hours 0–23, minutes 0–59, and the three identifiers. For invalid incoming data, retain the original record, identify the affected field, and require explicit correction before Save. Do not clamp or reinterpret it silently. A legacy blank repeat value maps to daily only when the legacy schema explicitly defines blank as Every day, as this brief does; do not treat arbitrary missing/corrupt data as daily.

## Time semantics and scheduling boundary

Use the watch'"'s current local time zone for future occurrences; a time-zone change preserves the chosen wall-clock hour/minute and named day set. Locale or calendar display changes reformat the same stored values without changing the schedule. Weekday membership is defined by the day sets above.

For this specification, the next reminder is the next eligible future local occurrence after Save; do not send a catch-up reminder for a time already passed. On a daylight-saving gap, skip a nonexistent occurrence; on a repeated local time, deliver once at the first occurrence. These are explicit product policies requiring scheduler validation, not HIG rules. Display the next occurrence on reminder detail after Save so the outcome can be reviewed. Medication identity and other reminder data remain unchanged.

## Acceptance contract

1. A saved 08:30 Every day opens with Hour 8, Minute 30, AM where applicable, and Every day selected. Adjusting Minute to 31 retains the hour and repeat choice through subsequent Crown events.
2. Every daily minute is representable. Check 00:00, 11:59, noon, and 23:59 in 12- and 24-hour locales; minute wrap does not carry into the hour. Noon and midnight retain the right stored hour when formatting changes.
3. Every day, Weekdays, and Weekends always have visible labels and exactly one selected value. Scrolling the summary or Repeat list does not commit a selection.
4. Done then Save persists the displayed time and repeat identifier together. Time Cancel, summary Cancel, saving failure, and interruptions follow the state rules above.
5. Invalid values cannot be silently saved; the documented legacy blank becomes explicit Every day. Locale, time-zone, Friday/weekend, DST gap, and repeated-time cases follow the stated semantics.
6. On a supported Watch, verify readable captions, unclipped localized labels, distinct selectable targets, touch equivalents, precise Crown selection, default haptic suitability, and no simultaneous page scrolling and value adjustment. These require runtime evidence.

## Design basis

The local HIG snapshot supports Crown-friendly watchOS wheels and navigation-link pickers, logical labeled values, and locale-aware time presentation: [Pickers — watchOS and best practices](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/pickers#watchOS). Keep the wrist task focused and navigation shallow: [Designing for watchOS](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/designing-for-watchos#Best-practices). Separate Crown adjustment from navigation and provide touch equivalents: [Digital Crown — Apple Watch](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/digital-crown#Apple-Watch). Use system buttons and explicit Save/Cancel outcomes: [Buttons](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/buttons#watchOS). Exact presets, defaults, commit boundaries, wrapping, and scheduling policies above are product decisions.
EOF"

# Revised medication reminder controls

Patched "'`interface.md` in place from a one-line problem statement into an implementable watchOS control specification. The patch replaces the unlabeled 1,440-value picker with labeled time wheels; makes Every day explicit; defines three named repeat choices; and adds draft persistence, Crown/touch mappings, Save/Cancel, validation, localization, and scheduling boundaries.

## Decisions and basis

- Use hour/minute wheels with optional AM/PM, retaining one-minute precision and all 1,440 time values. The brief requires a time of day, so a calendar date control adds no needed value. The installed [Pickers guidance](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/pickers#watchOS) supports watchOS wheels and locale-dependent display. It does not establish a particular SDK API or style/mode combination for this project.
- Use an explicit short single-selection list for Every day, Weekdays, and Weekends. The guide suggests simpler controls for short sets and supports watchOS navigation-link lists; direct named choices avoid numeric frequency encoding. The exact three presets and their day sets are proposed product scope because the supplied brief does not enumerate schedules.
